newsitem.title: USA: Storms impede TWA Flight 800 crash investigation.
newsitem.headline: Storms impede TWA Flight 800 crash investigation.

text.p: Storm-driven seas on Thursday hampered the hunt for clues in the crash of TWA Flight 800, keeping divers out of the water and sweeping the chief investigator overboard into the rough waves, officials said.
Investigators remained close-mouthed on any further evidence to support or rule out any of their three theories: that a bomb, missile or mechanical failure caused the plane to explode on July 17.
They have found microscopic traces of a chemical explosive on the debris, but say they need further evidence such as physical damage to draw a conclusion.

Hurricane Fran, several hundred miles (kilometers) south of the crash site off Long Island, New York, caused high swells and reduced visibility on the ocean floor to "zero-zero," Robert Francis, vice chairman of the National Transportation Safety Board, told a media briefing.
Francis said he had been riding in a boat with Rear Admiral Edward Kristensen on his way to board a U.S. Navy salvage ship when a "rogue wave" washed him overboard.
"Fortunately, the admiral was kind enough to turn around and come back and get me," he said with a wry smile.

While Francis has steadfastly refused to comment on most evidence, in response to a question he dispelled speculation that the Paris-bound Boeing 747 was hit by so-called friendly fire from U.S. military forces training nearby.
"There's no indication that that's the case," he said.
The Navy admiral said the nearest missile-equipped destroyer had been approximately 180 miles (290 km) from the crash site, out of firing range and not engaged in training or manoeuvres.
Francis also disputed the significance of two seats found with large holes in the backs that had been located near the centre of the plane where the explosion is believed to have occurred.

"Yes, there were holes in the back of these seats. I would also say there are lots of holes in almost everything that has any size at all," he said. "I would not put a whole lot of significance to that."
The storm is expected to keep divers out of the water until early next week, officials said.
Despite Hurricane Fran and Hurricane Edouard, which skirted the area earlier this week, wreckage on the ocean floor does not appear to have been disturbed a great deal, Kristensen said.
Francis also said he had made a trip to London to look at a mock-up of Pan Am Flight 103, which exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988 because of a bomb on board.
Investigators are reassembling wreckage from Flight 800 in an old aircraft hangar in Calverton, New York. About two-thirds of the plane has been recovered, Francis said.
All 230 people on board were killed. The bodies of 19 victims are still missing.
